reading.body:
FORBES-TATE's AI lobbying book is concentrated: two clients, CoreWeave and Universal Music Group, account for 28 of the 42 AI filings, and one lobbyist, Franklyn Steinberg, appears on 30.

The client list is the useful signal. CoreWeave is a GPU cloud provider, so its filings are compute infrastructure asking government for something. Universal Music Group and Imagine Learning are AI-adjacent content and education firms. The rest of the roster, Honda, the Bipartisan Policy Center, With Honor Action, is small by comparison, one filing each. This is not a broad tech-industry practice. It is a few AI-native clients plus a long tail.

The lobbyist counts show how the work is staffed. Steinberg at 30, Rachel Miller at 26, Cynthia Brown at 23, Elizabeth Greer and Richard Lopez at 22 each. A firm's AI practice is carried by a handful of named people, and the filings name them individually. Only one bill appears, S 2714, named in filings from 2025 or later.

What this does not show is position or outcome. A filing reports that a client lobbied on an issue, not what it argued or whether it won. The data covers one firm, one registrant id, and 42 reports. It says nothing about spending, and nothing about the compute buildout itself beyond the fact that a GPU cloud company is paying to be in the room.

summary: FORBES-TATE filed 42 Lobbying Disclosure Act reports on AI held by this site. Its clients, the lobbyists named on those filings and the AI bills they name are below. LDA registrant id 400976792.
